segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The morning of October the twenty-third, nineteen eighty-five, broke clear and cold over the Maine coast. The first hard frost of the year clung to the rails of the old lighthouse at Marsh Point. Inside, in the keeper's room, the wireless set crackled at twenty past six.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: Marsh Point, Marsh Point, this is Hawthorne. Eleanor, are you up there, over?

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: I'm here, Sarah. Coffee's on. I was waiting for you.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: Good morning, Gran. How's the air this morning?

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Cold. Clear. The water's flat as a pewter plate. You'd love it.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: I always do. Listen — the bureau's pushing the front in earlier than they said. They've moved the storm to twenty-two hundred your time. That's eight hours sooner than the call last night.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: ... I felt it would be. The gulls were quiet this morning.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: I knew you'd say that.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was a pause across the line. Sarah was thirty-two, working out of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. She had spent every summer of her childhood at this lighthouse. She had learned to read the sea from her grandmother before she had learned to read books.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: Gran. About this afternoon —

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: I know, dear. The ensign comes at fourteen hundred. They told me yesterday.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: I should be there. I should have come up last week.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: You should be where you are. It's only a lamp, Sarah. A lamp and a chair and a kettle.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: It's seventy-six years.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Seventy-six years of one lamp, one chair, and one kettle. The boat will come at fourteen hundred and a young man will sign a piece of paper and the lamp will become a relay. You can drive up next weekend and take me to the diner in Camden and we will sit there and eat a piece of pie and that will be the end of it.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: I love you, Gran.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: I love you too. Stay on the channel today, will you? I'd like to know the storm tracks the way the bureau says.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: I will. Marsh Point standing by. Hawthorne out.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The wireless went silent. Eleanor sat for a long moment with her hand still on the talk button. Then she stood up, slowly, and walked to the south window.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The morning sun had risen far enough to silver the edge of every wave. The horizon was clean. But the air had that particular taste — copper and salt and something else, something underneath — that the keepers of this point had learned to recognise across four generations.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Grandfather, you'd say it'll come at sixteen hundred. Won't you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She said it to no one in particular. Or so it seemed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The ensign's truck rolled up to the gate at thirteen fifty-three. Eleanor watched from the window as the young man climbed out, brushed off his coat, checked the time on his wristwatch, and adjusted his cap. He stood for a moment looking up at the tower. Then he walked to the door.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She opened it before he knocked.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: You're seven minutes early, Ensign.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: I'm — yes, ma'am. I — I wanted to make sure I wasn't late.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: You wouldn't have been late if you came in next Wednesday. Come in. The coffee's on.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Thank you, ma'am.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Eleanor. Or Mrs Marsh. Either will do. Ma'am makes me feel ninety.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... Mrs Marsh. Thank you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stepped inside. Jacob Cole, twenty-six years old, third in his class at the academy, two years in the Boston harbour, and now — to his bewilderment and quiet excitement — assigned the honour of retiring the last manual lighthouse keeper on the New England coast.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stood in the centre of the keeper's room and looked around. A black iron stove. A kettle. A bookshelf of marine almanacs. A logbook open on the desk, today's date already written at the top in fountain pen. A single chair by the south window, worn into the shape of one person.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... it's very nearly the way I imagined it.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Most people imagine it grander. They picture a kind of ocean cathedral. But it's mostly a kettle and a chair and a logbook. The lamp does its own work.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: The boat at fifteen hundred — they're delivering the relay unit.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: I know. There's a storm coming sooner than they said. Sit. Have your coffee first.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He sat. She poured him a cup.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: My grandfather built this stove. Eighteen ninety-nine. He carried the iron up the cliff in sections on his back. He said he wanted to be sure that whoever sat in the chair after him would always have warmth.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... Mrs Marsh, may I ask — how long have you been here?

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Since nineteen forty-six. Forty years next month. My father had it before me, my grandfather before him.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Three generations.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Four, in a sense. I had a son. He went to sea instead. He doesn't come up much. He didn't want the job.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was no bitterness in her voice. Only a kind of patient acceptance, as though she were reading a weather report.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: I'm sorry.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: For what? He has his own life. That's what we built the lamp for. So men out there could have their own lives.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The wind had begun to shift. The kettle made a small whistle that was the kettle's own, and another, distantly, that was not.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At sixteen hundred and twelve, the front came in.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The bureau had said twenty-two hundred. They were six hours wrong. The wireless went to static. The power blinked once and stayed off. The first hard rain hit the south window like a handful of nails.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Ensign. Move the chair. The lamp is mechanical from here. You're about to learn how the old lamp works.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Mrs Marsh — should I call the boat?

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: The boat won't come in this. They turned back forty minutes ago, whether they've told us or not. Light the lamp.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Light it — light it how?

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: With a match, Ensign. Like the rest of us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She walked up the spiral stairs. He followed. At the top, the great lens room. The brass mechanism. The wick. The oil. The match.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Two strikes. The flame caught. The lens picked it up. Sixteen seconds later, the beam swept north-east across the rain-blackened water for the first time in many years by human hand.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... I've read about this.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Now you've done it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They stood for a moment in the lens room, the rain hammering. Then Eleanor put her hand on the brass rail and looked through the south-facing window. Her face changed — only a little, but it changed.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Hello, Grandfather.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jacob followed her gaze. There was no one there. Only the rain on the empty walkway.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... Mrs Marsh?

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: He always comes when the weather turns bad.

segments.speaker: Thaddeus
segments.text: You look well, Ellie.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: You haven't said that to me since nineteen seventy-two.

segments.speaker: Thaddeus
segments.text: There's a vessel taking water. South-south-west. Eight nautical miles. She's lost her engines. The current's pulling her towards Cragg's Reef.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Eight miles. How fast?

segments.speaker: Thaddeus
segments.text: She'll be on the rocks in ninety minutes if no one finds her.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Mrs — Mrs Marsh, who are you talking to?

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: My grandfather, Ensign. Captain Thaddeus Marsh. He died on the walkway out there in nineteen oh-seven. In a storm not unlike this one.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... I don't —

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: You don't see him. I know. Most people don't.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She walked back down the stairs without further explanation. Jacob followed. At the wireless, she powered the emergency battery. Static. She turned the dial.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Marsh Point calling Coast Guard, Coast Guard, vessel in distress, vessel in distress.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Position south-south-west of Marsh Point, eight nautical miles. Drifting north-east on the current. Engine failure. Heading for Cragg's Reef. Repeat: heading for Cragg's Reef.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was a crackle, then a young man's voice on the channel.

segments.speaker: Coast Guard
segments.text: Marsh Point, this is Cutter Whitfield. We have no signal from any vessel in that quadrant. How do you have the position, over?

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: I have the position. They're not transmitting. Their radio is gone. Cutter Whitfield, you will find her exactly where I told you. Over.

segments.speaker: Coast Guard
segments.text: ... copy, Marsh Point. Proceeding to position. Out.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Eleanor sat back in the chair. Jacob stood near the window, looking out at the rain-blackened ocean. He could see nothing. Only the lens beam, sweeping across the night.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... Mrs Marsh.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: How did you know.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She did not answer immediately. She watched the lens beam complete one full rotation. Then she spoke.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Ensign. The lamp is mechanical. The wireless is wireless. But the keeper has always been — the keeper. You stand at this window for forty years. You learn to listen. Sometimes the dead help you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Forty-seven minutes later, Cutter Whitfield raised them on the channel.

segments.speaker: Coast Guard
segments.text: Marsh Point, Marsh Point. We have visual on a fishing vessel adrift. Three souls aboard. No engines, no radio, exactly where you said. Beginning rescue operation. Out.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... thank God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He sat down. Eleanor poured him another cup of coffee. The rain had begun to slacken.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Drink it while it's hot, Ensign. The storm's almost done.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Mrs Marsh — your grandfather.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: He died here.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: In nineteen oh-seven. There were four boats lost that night. He kept the lamp burning past midnight by hand, with the wick guttering, in a wind that took the slate off the roof. The next morning they found him on the walkway. The lamp was still lit. They said his heart had given out.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... I'm so sorry.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: He's never left. Not really. There's always been someone in the chair, and where there's a keeper there's a grandfather.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... is that why you took the job?

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: No, Ensign. I took the job because someone had to. The grandfather came with it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The rain stopped at thirty-six minutes past four in the morning. The wind dropped. The first thin band of grey appeared on the eastern horizon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Eleanor walked up the stairs one more time. Jacob followed. At the top, she turned out the wick. The lens room dimmed. The brass cooled.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Ensign. The relay arrives at fourteen hundred. You will sit through the day and the installation. Tomorrow at sunrise the automated light will come on. You will not need a match. The lamp will turn itself.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... yes, ma'am.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: But the keeper. The keeper has always been the one who watches the sea. The lamp is automated. The keeper, Ensign, is the one with the wireless and the chair. The keeper is still needed.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: I understand.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She turned and walked back down to the keeper's room. She sat in the chair by the south window. The sun had not yet risen. Her hands rested on the arms of the chair. She closed her eyes for a moment.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: Hello, Grandfather.

segments.speaker: Thaddeus
segments.text: Hello, Ellie. It's a good morning.

segments.speaker: Eleanor
segments.text: It is.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The sun crested the horizon at six-eleven. The room filled with a soft, even, gold-pink light. Eleanor Marsh did not open her eyes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jacob found her at six-twenty. She was sitting in the chair, facing south, her hands in her lap, her face perfectly calm. He stood in the doorway for a long moment. Then he walked to the wireless and powered it on.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Hawthorne, Hawthorne, this is Marsh Point. Sarah, are you there. Over.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was a pause. Then a young woman's voice came through, soft, already half-knowing.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: Marsh Point — Jacob — what is it.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Sarah. It's — your grandmother.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He could not say the next word.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: ... when.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: A few minutes ago. She was — she was watching the sunrise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The wireless crackled. Sarah did not cry. He could hear, faintly, that she was holding her breath. Then she let it out.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: ... thank you, Jacob.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: Tell her grandfather thank you, as well.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: ... I will.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The relay unit arrived at fourteen hundred that afternoon. Jacob signed the paperwork. He oversaw the installation. He stood with the engineers in the lens room and watched the automated mechanism come to life at sunset. The lamp turned. The beam swept across the water.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not leave. He sat in the chair by the south window for the rest of his rotation. The lamp turned itself. He watched the sea. The wireless was on. Once, in March of the following spring, he saw an old man in a Cornish fisherman's coat standing on the walkway, looking out at the morning fog. He raised his hand in salute. The old man smiled. By the time Jacob blinked, he was gone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jacob Cole served at Marsh Point for thirty-one years. He retired in two thousand and sixteen, at the age of fifty-seven, the longest serving keeper in the history of the post. The lamp had been automated for all those years.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the keeper, the keeper was the one who watched the sea.
